nameStory: The 'membranous pelt lichen' gets its name from its thin, membrane-like texture that feels delicate compared to other pelt lichens. Like all pelt lichens, it resembles an animal pelt or skin spread flat against its growing surface. The scientific name 'membranacea' comes from the Latin word for membrane, highlighting this species' distinctively thin, papery feel.
description: Membranous pelt lichen is a leafy (foliose) lichen that grows flat against rocks and soil like a green-gray animal hide. Its body forms lobed, leaf-like sections with distinctive vein-like markings that create a netted pattern across the surface. This medium-sized lichen can spread several inches across, feeling thin and papery to the touch. When fertile, it produces bright brown-orange, upright reproductive cups called apothecia that stand out dramatically against the muted body color.

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Feels distinctly thin and membrane-like, almost papery compared to other pelt lichens - you can sense its delicate nature when you gently touch it

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Leafy and flat-lying with distinct lobes that spread outward like fingers, creating a hand-like or pelt-like appearance against the substrate

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Grayish-green to brownish-green when dry, becoming more vibrant green when moist - the color change is quite noticeable after rain

idTips.label: Surface Pattern
idTips.description: Shows prominent vein-like markings that create a netted or reticulated pattern across the surface, though these aren't true veins

idTips.label: Reproductive Structures
idTips.description: Produces numerous bright brown-orange, cup-shaped apothecia that stand upright from the surface like tiny mushrooms

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Grows on rocks, soil, and moss, typically in areas with good air circulation and periodic moisture

habitat: Found on rocks, soil, and moss in areas with clean air and adequate moisture throughout New England. Prefers locations with good air circulation, often in partially shaded to open areas where it can receive periodic wetting from rain or dew. Most commonly encountered in upland areas away from heavy pollution.

seasonality.spring: Becomes more vibrant green with spring rains and may begin producing bright orange reproductive structures. The thin texture is especially noticeable when damp.
seasonality.summer: Appears more grayish and contracted during dry periods, but quickly revives and greens up after summer thunderstorms. Reproductive cups may be most prominent.
seasonality.fall: Maintains good color with autumn moisture and cooler temperatures. The vein-like pattern remains clearly visible as deciduous leaf litter settles around it.
seasonality.winter: Remains visible under snow and continues slow growth. May appear darker and more contracted, but the distinctive thin, membranous texture persists.

funFact: Despite having prominent vein-like markings that look just like leaf veins, these patterns have absolutely no vascular function - they're simply decorative ridges in the fungal tissue that mimic the appearance of true plant leaves!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other pelt lichens in the same genus, but the distinctly thin, papery feel sets it apart from thicker relatives like dog pelt lichen. Memory trick: 'membranous = membrane-thin' - if it feels substantially thick or leathery, it's probably a different pelt lichen species.
contextualKnowledge: This is one of the rarer pelt lichens in New England with only a couple of recorded observations, so finding one would be quite special. Pelt lichens are indicators of good air quality, so their presence suggests a healthy environment.
compareHints: Among the many pelt lichen species in New England, membranous pelt lichen stands out for its distinctly thin, papery texture - much more delicate than the thicker, more leathery dog pelt lichen or scaly pelt lichen. The bright brown-orange reproductive structures are more numerous and prominent than in many related species. Its vein-like surface pattern is similar to fan pelt lichen, but the overall thinner build helps distinguish it.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among the pelt lichens, scaly pelt is the only one in New England with prominent phyllidia scattered across its surface.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, horizontal pelt lichen is unique for its completely prostrate growth habit - it never curls up at the edges like dog pelt lichen or forms the ruffled, frilly margins of freckled pelt lichen.
Distinguished from dog pelt lichen by having many more fruiting structures along the edges rather than just a few large ones.

Among the many pelt lichens in New England, dog pelt lichen stands out for its preference for growing directly on soil rather than trees, and its particularly well-defined dark veining on a pale underside.
Among the pelt lichens, ruffled freckled pelt stands out for its notably bumpy, textured surface and strongly ruffled edges.
Unlike all other pelt lichens in New England, Eastern Waterfan is the only one that lives in water rather than on soil, rocks, or trees in terrestrial habitats.
Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has evenly-spaced, rounded lobes, alternating dog lichen has its distinctive alternating finger-like projections along the edges.
Among the pelt lichens, freckled pelt is the only one with distinctive dark green cephalodia (freckles), making identification fairly straightforward.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a smooth surface, peppered pelt is distinguished by its dark spotted pattern.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, sheepish pelt lichen is distinguished by its uniquely woolly surface texture - most other Peltigera species have smooth or slightly wrinkled surfaces.
Unlike the common dog pelt lichen which has a relatively uniform surface with veins on the underside, concentric pelt lichen displays obvious ring patterns on top.
Among the many pelt lichens in New England, field dog lichen stands out for its incredibly soft, velvety surface texture - most other dog lichens feel smoother or more leathery.
Carpet pelt lichen differs from its pelt lichen relatives by its consistently smooth upper surface and preference for soil rather than rocks or trees.
Unlike the smooth-surfaced dog pelt lichen or the powdery-edged freckled pelt lichen, mother-of-many pelt is immediately recognizable by its bumpy, phyllidia-covered surface.

Unlike the more common dog pelt lichen which has rounded, disk-like apothecia along the lobe edges, blacksaddle pelt has distinctive tubular, saddle-shaped reproductive structures on the lichen surface.

Compared to its Peltigera relatives, tree pelt lichen has a distinctly more velvety surface texture and tends to be more brownish in color than the grayer dog pelt lichen or the more distinctly veined fan pelt lichen.
Among its pelt lichen relatives, fan pelt lichen stands out with its smooth upper surface and distinctive raised black veins underneath.

Among pelt lichens, the pale-bellied pelt is distinguished by its consistently pale underside, whereas dog pelt lichen has a darker, often brownish underside with prominent veins, and freckled pelt lichen has distinctive dark spots on its upper surface.
